segments.source: For this guide, start with 18 grams of dry coffee and stop the espresso at 36 grams in the cup, then add 108 grams of hot water. The result weighs approximately 144 grams. These are Coffeedant’s suggested starting quantities for a conventional double basket, not a universal dark-roast specification. If your basket is designed for another dose, respect that capacity and scale the two ratios instead of squeezing 18 grams into every machine.

segments.source: Two shots can weigh the same and taste quite different. Two drinks can contain the same shot and feel quite different after dilution. Treating these as separate problems makes the next adjustment intelligible. A harsh espresso usually needs work before dilution. A pleasing espresso that makes a weak Americano may simply need less added water.

segments.source: Use the espresso range of a burr grinder with a conventional, unpressurized basket. There is no portable number of clicks: burr geometry, alignment, bean age and basket all change the result. The correct setting is the one that produces a repeatable, balanced shot at your chosen dose and yield. Record your own setting so tomorrow’s starting point has meaning.

segments.source: Going finer increases resistance, but finer indefinitely is not a reliable improvement.
segments.context: Going finer increases resistance, but finer indefinitely is not a reliable improvement. Barista Hustle’s Espresso Compass emphasizes even extraction and warns that an excessively fine grind can reduce it. This is why we begin with consistent distribution and a level tamp before repeatedly moving the grinder. Grind immediately before brewing, break up obvious clumps, spread coffee through the basket and tamp level.

segments.source: A practical first shot might land somewhere around 25–35 seconds from pump start, including any machine preinfusion. Use that window as a diagnostic note, not a pass mark. A well-balanced shot outside it can still be useful; an unpleasant shot inside it is not redeemed by the stopwatch. Always record how you counted time. Changing from pump start to first drip without saying so makes two otherwise identical recipes appear different.

segments.source: If your machine provides controlled brew-temperature adjustment, try approximately 90–92°C as an initial experiment for a developed dark roast, then taste. That range is an editorial starting suggestion, not a temperature measured on every bean. Keep dose and yield steady when comparing. If the cup is persistently smoky and drying, a small reduction is worth trying. If it becomes thin or sharply unbalanced, restore the previous setting before chasing a second variable.

segments.source: On a machine with no temperature control, a stable warm-up routine is more valuable than an invented temperature claim. Warm the portafilter, use the same preparation sequence and follow the manufacturer’s flushing guidance. Do not compensate for a cold machine by grinding extremely fine.

Taste a little of the espresso after it has cooled enough to assess. Then add water in measured stages. Begin with twice the espresso’s weight in water, taste, and move toward three or four times if you want a lighter drink. A 36-gram espresso with 72 grams of water makes a 108-gram drink; with 144 grams of water it makes 180 grams. The calculator turns these quantities into a repeatable recipe.

segments.source: Stir gently before comparing, and use the same cup and similar drinking temperature. Pouring espresso onto water changes how crema initially appears; adding water to espresso disperses it differently. Neither order rescues a poorly extracted shot. Choose the order that suits your workflow, then hold it constant while you compare concentration.

segments.source: Do not run the pump until the mug is full. That creates a different extraction, making it hard to know whether the final bitterness came from the coffee, the longer contact or the original preparation. Separate added water keeps the original espresso recipe legible.

segments.source: If the espresso tastes balanced but the diluted cup feels hollow, reduce water first. If the espresso races and tastes thin, a small finer adjustment is a reasonable next test with a conventional basket. If it barely flows, go coarser. If the coffee tastes uniformly burnt at several sensible recipes, the roast’s character may be the limitation. A grinder cannot reverse roasting.

This is enough to distinguish a useful experiment from random adjustments. Two consecutive similar shots matter more than an isolated spectacular one.

segments.source: Aromatic does not necessarily mean stronger. A concentrated cup can make roast bitterness dominate, while modest dilution may make its balance easier to notice. Your target is a drink that stays pleasant as it cools, not the darkest-looking liquid. The most useful dark-roast technique is restraint: extract a repeatable espresso, then choose how much room water gives it.
